doc.title: Carl Allen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, Georgia, January 4, 2013

title: Art Blakey's death and his upbringing
summary: Allen wept for three months after Blakey died and says Blakey cared more about men being responsible than about great musicians; Allen reflects on his rough orphan childhood.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: came from being with Art Blakey. And so I’ll never forget, man, the day that Art Blakey died boy, I told my wife, I said, “You know what, the music will never be the same.” I cried for three months. Every day. I mean I could just be watching TV or a soccer game come on and I’d hear Art’s voice and it had a profound effect on me. It really tore me up, man. He did so much for the music. Art’s thing was more about — and I heard him say this to guys many times — that he was more concerned with you growing up to be a man than to be a great musician. Because his thing was you’ve got to be responsible. You’ve got to do what you’re supposed to do.
Where did he learn that from? Do you have any idea?

Well I think, you knew Art grew up, he was an orphan, and he grew up I think kind of rough. He spent a lot of time around gangsters and all kind of rough folks, where he had to grow up fast. Now the irony of it is that you know, if you put his life on a plaque or a piece of paper, you wouldn’t say, oh that’s a great example of a positive role model, considering how many kids he had and all of that. But Art was, he really did a lot for a lot of people.
